## Who Snapback is for

Snapback is for people building real applications who want a backend that gets
out of the way at the prototype stage and stays with them into production.

The first-class product context is Contract/Exact app development, especially
mobile apps. React and Expo are important secondary consumers, but they should
not drive core design when their needs conflict with Contract/Exact.

The canonical Exact-side references are the Exact repository's
[`README.md`](../../exact/README.md) and [`AGENTS.md`](../../exact/AGENTS.md),
plus the Exact LLPs that define Contract, Contract's default-authoring policy,
and Design Mode: [Exact 0216](../../exact/llp/0216-contract-explained.explainer.md),
[Exact 0160](../../exact/llp/0160-contract-by-default.rfc.md),
[Exact 0158](../../exact/llp/0158-design-mode.rfc.md), and
[Exact 0200](../../exact/llp/0200-contract-design-mode-authoring-platform.rfc.md).
For Snapback-specific Contract data binding context, see [Exact 0263](../../exact/llp/0263-contract-data-bindings-for-snapback-and-backends.rfc.md)
and [Exact 0265](../../exact/llp/0265-contract-snapback-data-authoring-ergonomics.rfc.md).
Snapback should cite those sources rather than redefining Contract/Exact. The
known Snapback-side integration boundary is drafted in
[LLP 0005](./0005-contract-exact-react-integration.explainer.md) and specified
in [LLP 0012](./0012-headless-integration-contract.spec.md).

The first-class builder is an AI agent. Snapback's own implementation, generated
Snapback app code, and integration code should all assume agent authorship and
agent validation loops as the normal path. Human ergonomics are secondary to
giving agents strong affordances, tight feedback, and ways to get close to
guarantees.

A specific, important surface for that builder is Exact's **Design Mode** — where
an app is shaped by typing into a segment's chat box and turning knobs. Snapback
should integrate especially well with it. A useful design test for any Snapback
affordance: does a Design-Mode action (a sentence typed into a segment, a knob
turned) map cleanly onto the right backend behavior — the data read or written,
what syncs to the device, what updates live, who is allowed to see it — and is
that mapping legible enough for the agent to confirm it did the right thing? An
affordance that can't be driven well from Design Mode is a design smell.

The intended arc is one system across the whole lifecycle:

- **Prototype:** spin something up that costs ~nothing when idle and requires no
  infrastructure decisions.
- **Grow:** keep the same model and code as traffic increases.
- **Production:** carry a popular app without forcing a migration to a different
  stack. The north-star target is an app like Partiful reaching a few hundred
  thousand monthly active users on SQLite plus a lightweight JavaScript runtime
  (see [Scale targets and known limits](#scale-targets-and-known-limits)).

## Subsystems (v1)

These are the first-version building blocks. Each is sketched here at the
boundary level; the detailed design of each is expected to live in its own
follow-on LLP (see [Follow-on LLPs](#follow-on-llps)).

### Code execution

Backend logic runs as JavaScript. The runtime is pluggable:

- **Ibex** ([ccheever/ibex](https://github.com/ccheever/ibex)) for local
  deployments on your own machine and anywhere binary size matters.
- A **V8-based** runtime when running on Cloudflare, when you prefer it, or when
  you need its performance characteristics.

Both runtimes are *intended* to be interchangeable at the
programming-model level — the choice is meant to be an operational/target
decision, not a fork. That intent is **not yet earned**, but the mechanism that
earns it is now identified: a shared **runtime-conformance contract** (the
language/feature floor every acceptable engine must pass — see
[LLP 0009](./0009-code-execution-security.rfc.md) §Runtime Boundary), whose two
checkable properties are that the host can drive an `async` handler to
completion and does not hold the storage lock across async work. Valet's
`async`-handler rejection was an *execution-boundary* choice (synchronous eval
under the database lock), not an engine limit — Ibex already pumps the
microtask queue via `ex_hermes_poll` and Snapback adopts that boundary
([LLP 0003](./0003-local-code-hosting-and-storage-core.rfc.md) §Execution and
Write Semantics; [LLP 0006](./0006-valet-retrospective.research.md)). Until
that contract is implemented and verified, "one programming model" remains a
goal, not a property already in hand. Boa is not a Snapback engine option; only
Ibex and V8 are, unless a future, explicit reason names a third.

How executed code is isolated — the sandbox boundary around app code, and the
tenant-isolation model when one deployment serves multiple apps or is hosted for
other people — is a load-bearing constraint this explainer does not yet settle.
It is called out here and owned by a dedicated security follow-on (see
[Follow-on LLPs](#follow-on-llps)).

### Data storage

SQLite at the small scale, Postgres at the larger scale. The key constraint:
there is **one abstraction over both** that you use most of the time, so that
graduating from SQLite to Postgres is a mostly seamless transition rather than a
rewrite. Preserving that portability is a hard design requirement — anything
that makes the SQLite→Postgres move a rewrite has failed the brief.

The contract binds the shared abstraction: code written against it must move
from SQLite to Postgres without a rewrite. Reaching past it to engine-specific
features stays allowed — *paved path, not a cage* — but is an explicit opt-out
that trades away portability for that code. Where exactly the line sits, and
whether a portable subset is guaranteed, is for the storage LLP to pin down.

### Auth / login

For most apps, auth data is the most important data, and it is something teams
spend a lot of time setting up. Snapback treats it as first-class and keeps it
**next to the rest of your data**, so you can join it with your other tables,
query it, and export it freely. The paved path is a built-in system in the
spirit of WorkOS or Clerk; bringing your own provider (WorkOS, Clerk, or
anything else) is explicitly supported.

### Asset storage

Users want to upload photos and videos, so those are the priority, including a
**processing pipeline** for them. Other file types (PDFs, etc.) are supported
too, but photo/video processing drives the design. Asset bytes are normally
stored on the filesystem or in S3-style object storage as appropriate for where
you are hosting. Asset metadata, ownership, permissions, references, and
processing state live with the rest of the application data in SQLite/Postgres.

### Cron

Scheduled code execution. Every backend platform that matures grows this, so
Snapback includes it from the start.

### Notifications

Reach people by email, SMS, and push (and possibly other channels). This is a
**thin layer** that you configure with your own provider API keys, not a
reimplementation of those providers.

## Subsystems planned for v2 (post-launch)

These can wait until after the initial launch:

- **AI gateway** — call an AI API for something directly through Snapback.
- **Data gateway** — fetch data such as sports scores or weather through
  Snapback and pay for it where needed (sometimes free, sometimes paid).

## Cross-cutting requirements

These span every subsystem and are part of what makes Snapback distinct.

### Local-first with partial sync

Mobile apps must keep working offline, which means syncing the relevant slice of
data down to the device. The bar: a messaging app should still show your old
messages with no connection — the failure mode where WhatsApp would show *no*
messages offline is exactly what local-first exists to prevent. Full replication
is not assumed; **partial** sync of the data a given client needs is the model.

Desktop apps are an explicit case, not an afterthought, and they differ from
mobile in a way that matters here: far more data may live locally — a desktop
client might reasonably keep a large working set, or close to the whole dataset,
on disk. Partial sync therefore has to scale across a wide range of local-store
sizes, from a phone holding a thin slice to a desktop holding a great deal; the
sync model must not assume the mobile size profile.

### Realtime live updates

Changes should propagate to interested clients immediately. If someone RSVPs to
a party while another user is viewing the RSVP list, that guest should appear
under "Yes" and the count should increment without a refresh.

High-frequency transient state such as cursors, selections, typing indicators,
and online presence is realtime state too, but not ordinary durable data by
default. [LLP 0013](./0013-ephemeral-realtime-state.rfc.md) owns the proposed
ephemeral-state contract for that class: typed, TTL-bound latest-state
collections backed by process memory locally and adapter-specific infrastructure
on hosted targets.

### Multi-target deployment

Snapback should run on your own machine, your own hardware, Cloudflare, AWS,
Google Cloud, Azure, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Railway, and Fly.io. **Cloudflare is
unusual** enough that making Snapback work well there is called out as requiring
dedicated effort rather than being assumed to come for free. A runtime/deployment
LLP must define target profiles and launch requirements before agents treat the
whole matrix as implemented. Cloudflare is important enough that doing it well is
the planned second step after the local core (see
[Implementation order](#implementation-order)), and we should be open to
rearchitecting around its model rather than treating it as a port.

This is also where *scale to zero* has to be made precise. Idle cost is
target-dependent: a serverless or Cloudflare-style substrate can bill to
(almost) zero when idle, while an always-on VM — a Hetzner box, a cloud droplet
— keeps incurring its base rate no matter how light the app is. "Costs almost
nothing when idle" is therefore a property the architecture must earn per
target, not a universal guarantee; the deployment LLP should state what idle
cost looks like for each target profile. **The canonical local target's
entry is measured** ([LLP 0035](./0035-local-target-benchmarks.research.md)
§Idle cost, LLP 0032 X5): a provisioned idle instance performs zero disk
writes and no measurable CPU over a 120 s window, at ~13 MiB resident —
idle means idle on the process the architecture controls; the
dollars-when-idle question remains each target profile's to state.

**The All Aboard Cloudflare proof's no-subscriber entry is measured too.**
After an operator reset cleared the durable subscription registry, five status
observations established the demand-gated warm poll at `inactive:no-demand`,
demand zero, and no next or last run; the final observation at 2026-07-11
23:32:44Z defines the disarm boundary. Settled script-attributed Adaptive
analytics across the two request datasets over the pure 7,200-second quiet
window 2026-07-11 23:37:44Z–2026-07-12 01:37:44Z observed no rows, which the
reader summarized as **0 estimated Worker requests, 0 estimated Worker execution GB-s,
and 0 estimated Durable Object requests**. The account-wide periodic query
likewise observed no row, summarized as 0 µs of Durable Object active time.
The adjacent pre- and post-window controls returned nonzero rows through the
same queries, and a post-window query returned 21 stations while the refresh
action succeeded with source `511-siri-stop-monitoring`, so absent quiet-window
rows are not explained by attribution lag or a dead deployment. Cloudflare
documents that Adaptive datasets may be sampled, and an empty quiet result
carries no sample interval or confidence field, so this is one controlled
observed-zero estimate, not an absolute event-absence or invoice guarantee.
The raw aggregate and hourly evidence is
checked in as
[`measurements.remote.idle.2026-07-12.json`](../targets/cloudflare/generated/measurements.remote.idle.2026-07-12.json).
The Durable Object periodic/storage datasets lack script identity and remain
account-wide context; storage had no positive control and its empty array is
telemetry absence, not evidence of zero stored bytes. The per-script Worker and
Durable Object request datasets carry the deployment-specific observation.

## Canonical local target

Of all the targets, one is privileged as the **standard place to build and
test**: the whole server — code hosting *and* data store — running **locally on
your machine via Ibex + SQLite**. Other configurations are valid (for example,
running only the Wasm part of the sync engine in the browser), but this local
Ibex + SQLite server is the **first standard target** — the default an agent
assumes when it builds, runs, and validates its work, and the baseline the
[reference apps](#reference-apps) and their acceptance suite run against. The
decision and its consequences are recorded in
[LLP 0002](./0002-canonical-local-target.decision.md).

## Reference apps

These are concrete apps Snapback must be able to build *and run well* — the
working set the design is validated against, not just demos. Each leans on a
different mix of the subsystems and cross-cutting requirements above; together
they set the capability bar. (Some lean on
[v2 subsystems](#subsystems-planned-for-v2-post-launch) and are correspondingly
post-launch targets.)

- **Todo list** — the floor: basic CRUD, auth, and offline edits on the
  scale-to-zero prototype path. If this isn't trivial, nothing else matters.
- **1-1 and group messaging** (Signal/WhatsApp) — local-first with partial sync
  plus realtime delivery; the canonical "show old messages with no connection"
  case from [Local-first with partial sync](#local-first-with-partial-sync).
- **Kanban board** — realtime collaborative edits, optimistic reordering, and
  modest fan-out.
- **E-commerce store** — write correctness (inventory, orders) and asset storage
  for product media; also pulls in payments, an integration this corpus does not
  yet cover.
- **Collaborative whiteboard** — shared cursors and edits propagated *keystroke
  by keystroke*: the extreme realtime fan-out case, and exactly the
  [open fan-out question](#scale-targets-and-known-limits) this corpus has not
  yet answered.
- **Collaborative rich-text pad** — a small focused multiplayer editor across
  platforms. This is a nice-to-have stress case distinct from the Notion-like
  workspace: it asks whether Snapback can support at least one good approach to
  rich-text collaboration — operation log, CRDT/OT bridge, block-level mutations,
  or another explicit design — with cursor/selection presence, offline replay,
  and realtime convergence. It does not require Snapback's ordinary row-sync
  model to solve every editor architecture automatically.
- **Task tracker** (Linear) — local-first partial sync over a large dataset, with
  a snappy offline UX as the bar.
- **Notion-like workspace** — documents-plus-databases with realtime collab and a
  large local dataset, especially on desktop: a stress test for local-first at
  scale (the [desktop](#local-first-with-partial-sync) large-local-data case) and
  for flexible, structured-and-freeform data.
- **Team chat / community hub** (a mini Slack or Discord) — channel-scale
  realtime fan-out, presence, history partial-sync, and notifications. A mini
  version is fine; we don't need every feature.
- **Social / video app** (TikTok/YouTube/Instagram/Twitter) — the
  [asset storage](#asset-storage) and processing pipeline at scale, plus
  read-heavy feed fan-out; the photo/video-first case that subsystem targets.
- **Blog** — read-heavy content with image assets; web is a secondary client
  target but should still be served well.
- **Multiplayer card game** — each player sees a different view (secret hands), so
  partial sync must be **authorization-aware** — syncing only what a viewer is
  permitted to see — over realtime, server-authoritative state.
- **Party app** (Partiful) — RSVP realtime and invite/reminder notifications;
  already the north-star [scale target](#scale-targets-and-known-limits).
- **Finance app** (Robinhood/Coinbase) — money-grade write correctness, realtime
  price reads, sensitive-data auth, and external market data (a **v2** data
  gateway consumer).
- **Daily-fantasy / fantasy-sports picker** — scheduled scoring and contest locks
  via Cron, realtime leaderboards, and external sports data (a **v2** data
  gateway consumer).

The aim is breadth of *kind*, not a feature-complete clone of each: together
they exercise every v1 subsystem and every cross-cutting requirement, and they
push the realtime, correctness, and asset axes to their edges. What "works well"
means for each is acceptance-suite work for a follow-on LLP.

## Non-goals

Setting expectations is part of the design. Snapback is **not** trying to be
excellent at the following, and we'd rather say so up front. (You may still be
able to build a small version of some of these — they just aren't what the system
is optimized for, and they must not steer the design.)

- **Fast-twitch realtime games** — massively-multiplayer first-person shooters
  and other fast-action multiplayer games that stream large volumes of
  positional state at high tick rates. These want authoritative low-latency game
  servers, not a SQLite-backed sync model.
- **Serverless mesh sync — apps that must work with no server, ever** (named
  2026-07-23, LLP 0086 CC-8 row 13). Offline-critical physical operations —
  aircraft cabins, restaurant floors, contested networks — where devices must
  keep syncing peer-to-peer with no server reachable are a real, paying
  segment, and it is the one place CRDT convergence is the only correct tool;
  Ditto serves it and pays the structural price (certificate-carried
  permissions over immutable fields, conflicts resolved at read time)
  ([LLP 0084](./0084-triplit-ditto.research.md) §Findings, §Synthesis).
  Snapback is server-authoritative by design: its offline story is client
  replicas and mutation replay against an authoritative backend, and its
  "local-first" language must never blur into a no-server mesh claim. This
  marker plays the same boundary-naming role as the fast-twitch-games bullet
  above and LLP 0001's SpacetimeDB and Nakama/Colyseus markers.
- **High-frequency write firehoses** — clickstream/ad-tech ingestion, large-scale
  IoT telemetry, or matching engines sustaining very high write rates. That
  throughput profile fits neither the small-scale stack nor the scale-up target.
- **Analytics / data-warehousing workloads** — heavy OLAP over huge datasets
  belongs in a warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHouse). Snapback's store is
  transactional and app-facing, not an analytics engine.
- **CDN-scale streaming infrastructure** — being the global live-video transcode
  and delivery backbone. Building an app that *hosts and plays* user video is in
  scope (see the social/video reference app); being a streaming CDN is not.
- **Heavy compute / ML training** — GPU training jobs and large batch-compute
  pipelines. Snapback runs app logic and should call out to dedicated services
  for these.

These are starting expectations, not a final boundary; the ratifying source can
prune or extend the list as the scale-up envelope is benchmarked.

## Design principles and non-obvious constraints

Future work is expected to honor these even when they are inconvenient.

- **Scale to zero, then scale up.** Lightness at idle is a primary design goal,
  not an afterthought. The same system must still scale up to a popular
  production app.
- **Comprehensive and coherent.** Prefer one roof where the pieces are designed
  together over a loose collection of services. The Rails comparison is
  intentional.
- **Paved path, not a cage.** Let people do whatever they want, but make the
  blessed ways of doing things work exceptionally well. Bring-your-own
  alternatives (e.g. external auth providers) should remain possible.
- **Agent-first developer experience.** We expect essentially all Snapback
  framework code, generated app backend code, and integration code to be written
  by AI agents. Agent DX is therefore the priority, and where it trades off
  against human ergonomics, agent DX wins. Concretely, the syntax, tooling, and
  APIs should give agents ways to get *close to guarantees* about what they
  intend, and should provide **complete feedback loops** so an agent can
  validate its own work and understand the current state of the system.
  (`ref-check`, run by both agents and CI, is an early example of this
  feedback-loop philosophy applied to the design corpus itself.)
- **Contract/Exact first; React/Expo a strong second.** The primary client
  target is the Contract/Exact app stack, and its needs drive core design
  decisions. React and Expo are first-class *secondary* consumers — supported as
  well as they can be, but not steering the design.
- **Truly open.** MIT licensed. No "funny business" source-available licenses
  that prevent hosting Snapback for other people.

## Scale targets and known limits

- **Target:** SQLite + Ibex should carry an app like Partiful to a few hundred
  thousand monthly active users. That is the goal the small-scale stack is being
  designed against, not yet a proven benchmark.
- **Needs definition:** the workload envelope must be specified before this
  becomes an engineering claim: concurrent users, reads/sec, writes/sec,
  realtime subscription fan-out, asset upload volume, cron load, notification
  throughput, latency targets, and acceptable degradation behavior.
- **Benchmark gate:** every reference-app family that is used to claim scale
  must have an acceptance profile with data shape, local-store size, mutation
  rate, subscription count, fan-out pattern, and degradation behavior. A demo
  proves product shape; a benchmark proves the scale claim. The runnable demo
  corpus and its Contract/Exact dependency policy are planned in
  [LLP 0015](./0015-demo-application-suite.plan.md).
- **Out of scope:** several workloads are explicit non-goals — fast-twitch
  realtime games, write firehoses, analytics warehouses, and more — collected under
  [Non-goals](#non-goals).
- **Open question:** the upper bound on high-frequency fan-out is not yet known
  — e.g. whether ~100 people on the same site, each with a continuously synced
  mouse position pushed out to every other client, is realistic on this stack.
  This needs empirical answers, ideally informed by what was learned from Valet.

## Lessons from Valet

Snapback's predecessor was **Valet** ([expo/valet](https://github.com/expo/valet)),
an earlier prototype whose general architecture remains directionally important:

- A small **Rust** service running alongside **SQLite**, executing your code and
  using SQLite for storage, is considered directionally correct.
- For the code engine, **Ibex** is fine, and **V8** should also work well.
- Empirical testing of Valet ran into real problems that made it hard. Those
  specific problems have now been recovered from Valet's experience diaries and
  LLP corpus in [LLP 0006](./0006-valet-retrospective.research.md), then
  promoted into the storage, sync, runtime, auth, DX, and integration LLPs. The
  recovered record is strong enough to constrain v1: no silent codegen drops, no
  handler source-only replay, no per-row version triggers for one logical
  mutation, no silent backpressure drops, no stale subscription initial state, no
  typecheck theater, and no pretending Ibex/Hermes can enforce hosted-code
  resource limits until it actually can. What remains unanswered is not the
  basic failure list but the production envelope: single-writer breaking point,
  fan-out ceiling, retention/matcher cost, hosted isolation, and idle-cost
  behavior by target.

## Implementation order

Direction, not a schedule. Build it in this order, with the first step treated as
a **narrow proof**, not as a compressed version of the whole product:

1. **Code hosting + data storage first, on Ibex + SQLite.** Get the core — your
   code running and your data stored — solid on the
   [canonical local target](#canonical-local-target) before broadening anything
   else. It is the foundation every other subsystem sits on. The first-slice
   architecture is split across
   [LLP 0003](./0003-local-code-hosting-and-storage-core.rfc.md) for the local
   Rust server and SQLite core, and
   [LLP 0004](./0004-application-data-api.rfc.md) for the application data API
   that apps and agents use.
2. **Then Cloudflare, done well.** Once the core feels good, the next move is to
   make Snapback work *well* on Cloudflare — which may mean more than a port.
   Cloudflare's model is unusual enough (see
   [Multi-target deployment](#multi-target-deployment)) that we should be open to
   **rearchitecting around how Cloudflare works** rather than bolting it onto a
   design shaped only by the local stack.

The **first implementation slice** is deliberately smaller than the v1 product
surface. It should prove:

- one trusted local app on Ibex + SQLite;
- generated schema and function artifacts loaded by the local server;
- one portable single-table indexed query shape;
- one server-authoritative mutation path with one atomic commit version;
- a named mutation isolation strategy, so reads performed before commit cannot
  silently violate invariants under concurrent writes;
- one syncable live-query subset with an authoritative initial snapshot and
  online realtime deltas;
- deterministic reset/seed and machine-readable diagnostics;
- a headless or React fixture that consumes the generated contract without
  Contract/Exact-private backend semantics.

That first slice should **not** claim offline mutation replay, hosted/untrusted
execution, Postgres graduation, Cloudflare, real auth providers, assets, cron,
notifications, rich text, high-frequency whiteboard fan-out, finance-grade money
semantics, or Design Mode authoring. Those later capabilities must appear as
explicit capability gaps, not as half-implemented hidden behavior.

Cloudflare remains the planned second target, but it needs its own strategy LLP
before the local core hardens around unportable assumptions. At minimum that
strategy should identify the target seams for connection ownership, change
notification, durable state, scheduler/alarm behavior, WebSocket/session
lifetime, runtime isolation, secrets, asset storage, and storage-engine choice.
That strategy is drafted as
[LLP 0014](./0014-cloudflare-strategy.rfc.md).

Everything else — the rest of the deployment matrix, the v2 subsystems, and the
broader reference-app set — follows once the narrow local proof and the Cloudflare
strategy are in hand.

## Repository and LLP setup

This repository keeps its LLP corpus directly in [`llp/`](../llp), rather than
using an LLP submodule for the documents themselves. The agent-facing rules are
in [`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md), validation is via [`ref-check`](../ref-check)
(also run in CI), and the project skill aggregate lives under
[`skills/`](../skills/).

The skill files in `skills/` are symlinks into branch-tracking upstream
submodules under [`vendor/llp`](../vendor/llp) and
[`vendor/ccheever-skills`](../vendor/ccheever-skills), then exposed to each
agent through that agent's project-local skill directory. Run
[`scripts/sync-agent-skills`](../scripts/sync-agent-skills) after updating the
upstream skill repos. The LLP workflow itself is maintained at
<https://github.com/ccheever/llp>.

## Status

This is a living document and the root of the corpus. It will change as
subsystem boundaries firm up and as follow-on LLPs settle the provisional
choices noted above. Update it — and land the update with the change that
motivated it — whenever the project's intent or top-level structure moves.

**Type:** RFC
**Status:** Draft
**Systems:** Snapback 4 web client, app identity and readiness, online and local observations, durable browser writes, WASM loading, React, SSR
**Author:** Codex, requested by Charlie Cheever
**Date:** 2026-10-29

**Related:** [LLP 3000.002](./3000.002-end-to-end-resource-bounds.research.md#browser-startup-loading), [LLP 3000.013](./3000.013-quarry-states-intent.rfc.md#6-a-paved-client), [LLP 3000.013.000](./3000.013.000-a-browser-write-journal-without-the-device.rfc.md), [LLP 3000.001](./3000.001-durable-replica-and-write-lifecycle.research.md), [LLP 3000.001.000](./3000.001.000-device-engine-handshake.rfc.md), [LLP 3000.023](./3000.023-answers-stay-on-screen.rfc.md), [LLP 3000.028](./3000.028-one-query-online-or-offline.rfc.md), [LLP 3000.038.000](./3000.038.000-durable-offline-media-intents.rfc.md)

## 1. Proposal

A local-first Snapback web app should show authorized data and accept durable
ordinary writes without downloading or initializing the local interpreter.
It should gain local execution, prediction and offline reads in the background,
through the same application object and hooks. A returning device with usable
local state should take the faster local path, including when offline.

The desired end state remains under 100 KB for all compressed SDK JavaScript
and WASM needed for full local operation, excluding the app and React. This
RFC uses a sub-100-KB initial gzip budget as a near-term fallback; deferred
bytes still count toward the full runtime, whose size remains separate work.

Make these three events independent:

1. The application has established its current identity and durable authority.
2. The application can serve useful data and own new writes.
3. The local runtime and replica can take over the relevant work.

Keep the shared Rust interpreter and the complete local feature set. Use the
existing online client and browser admission mechanisms for the first phase.
Prefer giving the existing local client a late-bound core, so that its existing
publication procedure decides when a local answer may replace a server answer
(§6), over a new coordinator arbitrating between two clients. Keep one write
dispatcher per document, with local takeover decided at the next open (§7.2).
Do not construct two independent apps and swap them.

This RFC proposes a behavioral change, not another packaging-only optimization.
The author requested it after observing that roughly seven seconds to first
local data remained unacceptable. Writing this Draft does not commission its
implementation or establish that the proposed latency targets have been met.

## 2. Evidence and the failure of the byte-only target

The 2026-10-29 change landed at `5913715c25`. It reduced the representative
initial SDK graph below 100 KB and improved WASM preparation. It did not remove
the local engine from the path to a signed-in app's first data.

| Measurement | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Representative initial SDK, gzip | 122,882 B | 82,432 B |
| Representative initial SDK, Brotli | 103,383 B | 70,929 B |
| Full WASM device, gzip | 741,502 B | 741,502 B |
| First contentful paint, median | 1,012 ms | 788 ms |
| First local inbox result, median | 6,901 ms | 6,514 ms |

The byte measurement retains common app/auth/device/React-hook imports and
excludes React and authored UI. The timing probe is a smaller production-built
persona page without React, with three fresh browser contexts per variant in
alternating order: Chromium 151.0.7922.34, gzip, 1.6 Mbps download, 150 ms
latency and 4× CPU throttling. These are different fixtures. The timing probe's
inbox was empty; it is evidence of a startup delay, not a qualification of a
useful populated screen or production authentication.

In the resulting trace, the WASM request starts around 1.33 s and finishes
around 5.19 s. First data follows around 6.51 s. About 3.86 s is transfer and
another 1.32 s follows the download. At that throughput, even an ideal transfer
of the gzip device takes about 3.7 seconds before latency or initialization.
The smaller initial graph improved paint while leaving the principal problem.

The raw samples, artifact identity and scope are retained in
[`metrics/client.jsonl`](../snapback4/metrics/client.jsonl) and
[`metrics/witness.jsonl`](../snapback4/metrics/witness.jsonl), with the analysis
in the parent research. The prior completion claim applied only to the
initial-download fallback; it did not satisfy fast first usable data.

The browser device is the Rust interpreter over memory, persisted through
IndexedDB. It does not carry SQLite. Removing SQLite is therefore not a way
to remove this download.

## 3. Existing mechanisms and constraints

The current paved surface is recorded in
[`CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS.md`](../snapback4/packages/snapback4/reference/CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS.md).
The relevant implementation boundaries are:

- [`app.ts`](../snapback4/packages/snapback4/src/app.ts) opens a provisional
  local client before publishing its signed-in scope. Its `online` arm is
  attached to that published owner, so it is not an early-read escape hatch.
- [`client-start.ts`](../snapback4/packages/snapback4/src/client-start.ts)
  separates prepare, commit and activate. Extend that ownership model instead
  of letting two independently restoring clients race to own the session.
- [`app-online.ts`](../snapback4/packages/snapback4/src/app-online.ts) and
  [`online-capture.ts`](../snapback4/packages/snapback4/src/online-capture.ts)
  already support durable browser writes without the interpreter. The online
  journal and device outbox are distinct recovery owners today.
- [`react.tsx`](../snapback4/packages/snapback4/src/react.tsx) follows the app's
  client and auth publications. Keeping these identities stable matters for
  mounted observations, forms and pending-write handles.

The implemented authority, custody and observation rules remain binding:

- Durable session replacement, logout epochs, credential fencing and
  cross-tab checks follow [LLP 3000.013 §6](./3000.013-quarry-states-intent.rfc.md#6-a-paved-client).
  A localStorage credential mirror is not authority.
- A browser write needs synchronous capture and durable recovery under
  [LLP 3000.013.000](./3000.013.000-a-browser-write-journal-without-the-device.rfc.md).
  A promise queued only in memory is not a captured write.
- Read retention follows the current amendments in
  [LLP 3000.023](./3000.023-answers-stay-on-screen.rfc.md), including §12.
  A transition must not prolong stale authorization or restart a retention deadline.
- Local execution still needs the actual device's
  [engine handshake](./3000.001.000-device-engine-handshake.rfc.md).
  Server answers cannot stand in for a compatible local engine.
- [The scope fence](../snapback4/NOT-DOING.md) keeps one Rust interpreter,
  declared-partition replication and the existing read vocabulary. This
  proposal adds no persistent per-query result cache or second interpreter.

## 4. Readiness and the authoring surface

**Author ruling, 2026-10-30:** "land it and make it the default". This overrides
the earlier qualification-before-default order: Lane D makes progressive startup
the default now; Lane C qualifies afterward. The latency targets in §9 remain
unqualified by this change.

`createApp` accepts `startup?: "progressive" | "awaited"`. With a custody probe
(`webDevice()`), omission means progressive startup. Openers without that probe
(native/Expo) always retain awaited opening. Either explicit startup mode
without a device returns a typed `E_CLIENT` refusal and rewrite; `writes: "online"`
with a device remains refused.

```ts
const app = createApp({
  url,
  sessionStore: localStorageSessionStore(),
  device: webDevice({ worker: true }),
  // startup: "awaited" restores the previous device-opening barrier.
});
```

`AppProvider`, `useQuery`, `usePage`, `useMutation`, `usePendingWrites` and the
ordinary app methods keep selecting the execution path internally. A builder
does not maintain duplicate online/local screens, subscriptions or mutation ids.

| Surface | Default meaning for web apps (progressive mode) |
|---|---|
| `auth.state` | Identity and authority state. Engine download alone does not keep a validated scope `restoring`. |
| `app.ready` | Initial restoration has established a usable client and the required write-custody gate, or returned a typed refusal. It does not promise a complete replica. |
| `Read<T>` | The existing data/loading/denied contract, with truthful completeness, freshness, expiry and revalidation metadata. |
| `client.acquired` | Its existing replica acquisition meaning. A server answer does not set it. |
| `localStatus(client)` / `useLocalStatus()` | `loading`, `opening`, `syncing`, `ready` or `unavailable`, with `executable`, `acquired` and a typed cause where relevant. Useful for an offline indicator, not required around every query. |

The local-status API distinguishes an executable engine from an acquired
replica; write ownership follows §7.2. Compilation alone is not full offline
readiness. These observations work in both startup modes.

Asset hooks keep a retryable opening `E_STORE` in loading and subscribe to
local status as well as link changes. Executable/acquired notifications retry
only that unresolved opening read; a permanent opening failure surfaces its
typed refusal. Successful handles and all other asset outcomes retain their
existing lifetime and retry rules. Kept upload observations likewise refresh
when local storage becomes executable; no user action is automatically replayed.

Callers needing `app.ready` as the old local-opening barrier explicitly select
`startup: "awaited"`. Both modes inspect and recover existing journal custody;
only the engine-opening barrier differs. An awaited compatible opening with an
empty journal and no unsettled capture may select the outbox even on a first
visit. Starters omit the option; the cards document the opt-out.
Lane D audits the shipped readiness documentation and samples with the flip;
qualification is subsequent work under the ruling above.

## 5. Startup paths

### 5.1 First visit with a network

1. Load the small SDK and render the application.
2. Establish identity, authoritative session state, backend store identity and
   admission ownership using the online path. Reuse metadata on existing
   authenticated responses where possible. Do not require the full schema,
   partition snapshot or engine stamp to authorize a server read. If the
   existing replies lack sufficient bootstrap metadata, add a small validated
   envelope; do not substitute an unauthenticated local hint.
3. Publish the usable app and run foreground queries through the online client.
   Ordinary mutations use the durable host journal described in §7.
4. Load and prepare the complete local runtime in the background. Normally
   start the bulk download after the first foreground result, so it does not
   compete with that result for a slow connection. If there is no foreground
   read, begin after the initial render. Use a bounded scheduling policy so
   a stalled read or continuously busy page cannot starve local preparation;
   its timeout and bandwidth tradeoff must be measured, not assumed.

const home = type => ({ store_id: "media-store", table: "messages", row: "message", column: "photo", generation: 1, expiresAt: null, type });

for (const coordinate of ["store_id", "table", "row", "column", "missing"]) test(`an invalid ${coordinate} receipt cannot erase another confirmed entry`, async t => {

  assert.ok(kept?.url);
  const before = await readFile(files.bytesPath("photo"));
  const reply = response({ type: "image/png" });
  if (coordinate === "missing") reply.headers.delete("x-snapback-asset-home");
  else reply.headers.set("x-snapback-asset-home", encodeURIComponent(JSON.stringify({ ...current, [coordinate]: "old" })));
  await cache.viewed("photo", new Blob(["old"], { type: "image/png" }), reply);
  assert.deepEqual(await readFile(files.bytesPath("photo")), before);
  kept.revoke(); await cache.close();
  const reopened = await files.open();
  const retained = await reopened.cache.read("photo"); assert.ok("url" in retained); retained.revoke();
});

test("an invalid receipt for the confirmed entry's own cell retires it", async t => {
  const files = await deviceFiles(t);
  files.homes.set("photo", home("image/png"));
  const { cache } = await files.open();
  const kept = await cache.viewed("photo", new Blob(["bytes"], { type: "image/png" }), response({ type: "image/png" }));
  assert.ok(kept?.url);
  files.homes.delete("photo");
  await cache.viewed("photo", new Blob(["old"], { type: "image/png" }), response({ type: "image/png" }));
  assert.deepEqual(await files.manifest(), []);
  await assert.rejects(readFile(files.bytesPath("photo")), { code: "ENOENT" });
});

for (const type of ["image/png", "video/mp4"]) test(`native ${type} bytes survive a fresh cache opener; response ownership ends after copying`, async t => {
  const readers = installReader(t), urls = installUrls(t), files = await deviceFiles(t);
  const bytes = [0, 255, 128, 4, 9], blob = nativeBlob(bytes, type);
  files.homes.set("photo", home(type));
  const { core, cache } = await files.open();
  const originalWrite = core.media.write;
  core.media.write = async (...args) => { assert.equal(blob.closes, 0); await originalWrite(...args); assert.equal(blob.closes, 0); };
  const result = await fetchBlob(blob, (body, reply) => cache.viewed("photo", body, reply));
  assert.equal(result.url, core.media.uri("photo"));
  assert.equal(result.type, type);
  assert.equal(result.bytes, bytes.length);
  assert.equal(blob.closes, 1, "the retained file replaces the response Blob");
  assert.deepEqual([...await readFile(new URL(result.url))], bytes);
  result.revoke(); result.revoke();
  assert.deepEqual([...await readFile(files.bytesPath("photo"))], bytes, "releasing a file handle keeps ordinary cached bytes");
  await cache.close();
  const reopened = await files.open();
  const held = await reopened.cache.read("photo");
  assert.deepEqual([...await readFile(new URL(held.url))], bytes);
  held.revoke();
  assert.equal(readers.length, 1);
  assert.equal(readers[0].onload, null);
  assert.deepEqual(urls.created, [], "native retained files need no Blob URL");
});

for (const receipt of ["valid", "absent", "malformed", "incomplete", "no table", "no row", "no column"]) test(`once responses with ${receipt} receipts remove stale ordinary bytes without reading or storing the once Blob`, async t => {
  const readers = installReader(t), urls = installUrls(t), files = await deviceFiles(t);
  files.homes.set("photo", home("image/png"));
  const { core, cache } = await files.open();
  // Exercise live Blob URL revocation as well as removal of the durable file.
  delete core.media.uri;
  const viewed = (body, reply) => cache.viewed("photo", body, reply);
  const ordinary = await fetchBlob(nativeBlob([1, 2]), viewed);
  const once = nativeBlob([3, 4]);
  const reply = response(once, "none");
  if (receipt === "absent") reply.headers.delete("x-snapback-asset-home");
  if (receipt === "malformed") reply.headers.set("x-snapback-asset-home", "%not-json");
  if (receipt === "incomplete") reply.headers.set("x-snapback-asset-home", encodeURIComponent(JSON.stringify({ store_id: "old-store" })));
  // Each coordinate alone: an old store's receipt missing it cannot protect current bytes.
  if (receipt.startsWith("no ")) {

    delete partial[receipt.slice(3)];
    reply.headers.set("x-snapback-asset-home", encodeURIComponent(JSON.stringify(partial)));

  assert.equal(readers.length, 1, "once bytes must not enter byte extraction");
  assert.deepEqual(files.writes, ["photo"]);
  assert.deepEqual(await files.manifest(), []);
  await assert.rejects(readFile(files.bytesPath("photo")), { code: "ENOENT" });
  assert.deepEqual(urls.revoked, [ordinary.url], "the live ordinary handle loses its bytes");
  assert.equal(once.closes, 0, "the transient view owns its live native Blob");
  result.revoke(); result.revoke();
  assert.equal(once.closes, 1);
  assert.deepEqual(urls.revoked, [ordinary.url, result.url]);
  await cache.close();
  const reopened = await files.open();
  assert.equal((await reopened.cache.read("photo")).denied.code, "E_OFFLINE");
});

  if(u.state==="cancelling")return {id:entry.id,state:"cancelling",...(u.why?{why:u.why}:{})};

## Durable offline capture

For custody without waiting for reconnect:
```ts
import { hasUploads, uploadAndPlace } from "snapback4/local";
if (hasUploads(client)) {
  const write = await uploadAndPlace(client, api.placePhoto, {title}, file, {argument: "photo", waitSeconds: 0});
  // Keep the draft until sent; queued/uploading/placing are not success.
}
```
The placement mutation takes the named asset argument; online-only clients use client.upload then placement. Full recipe: guide package-reference offline-uploads.

`useUpload` and `uploadAndPlace` commit a byte copy and its placing mutation
together to the device outbox. For the API, Exact adapter contract, typed
states, native save and WAV/MP3/FLAC file types, read the package's
`guide package-reference offline-uploads`.

`E_CANCELLED`: the save/share sheet was cancelled. Call `saveAsset` again
when the user wants to retry.

`E_UPLOAD`: an upload is held without a recorded reason. Retry the same intent
or discard it before placement dispatch.

`E_UPLOAD_DEVICE`: pass `webDevice()` or Expo's `nativeDevice` to `createApp`;
the online-only client has no durable capture capability.

`E_UPLOAD_BYTES`: select nonempty bytes of at most 64 MiB; capture copies the
selected range before delivery.

`E_UPLOAD_ARGUMENT`: omit one declared image/video/file mutation argument,
name it in `argument`, and keep the other encoded args within 64 KiB.

`E_UPLOAD_QUOTA`: unresolved device or pinned owner bytes exceed 128 MiB.

`createApp` accepts `startup?: "progressive" | "awaited"`. With a custody probe
(`webDevice()`), omission means progressive startup. Openers without that probe
(native/Expo) always retain awaited opening. Either explicit startup mode
without a device returns a typed `E_CLIENT` refusal and rewrite; `writes: "online"`
with a device remains refused.

```ts
const app = createApp({
  url,
  sessionStore: localStorageSessionStore(),
  device: webDevice({ worker: true }),
  // startup: "awaited" restores the previous device-opening barrier.
});
```

`AppProvider`, `useQuery`, `usePage`, `useMutation`, `usePendingWrites` and the
ordinary app methods keep selecting the execution path internally. A builder
does not maintain duplicate online/local screens, subscriptions or mutation ids.

| Surface | Default meaning for web apps (progressive mode) |
|---|---|
| `auth.state` | Identity and authority state. Engine download alone does not keep a validated scope `restoring`. |
| `app.ready` | Initial restoration has established a usable client and the required write-custody gate, or returned a typed refusal. It does not promise a complete replica. |
| `Read<T>` | The existing data/loading/denied contract, with truthful completeness, freshness, expiry and revalidation metadata. |
| `client.acquired` | Its existing replica acquisition meaning. A server answer does not set it. |
| `localStatus(client)` / `useLocalStatus()` | `loading`, `opening`, `syncing`, `ready` or `unavailable`, with `executable`, `acquired` and a typed cause where relevant. Useful for an offline indicator, not required around every query. |

The local-status API distinguishes an executable engine from an acquired
replica; write ownership follows §7.2. Compilation alone is not full offline
readiness. These observations work in both startup modes.

Asset hooks keep a retryable opening `E_STORE` in loading and subscribe to
local status as well as link changes. Executable/acquired notifications retry
only that unresolved opening read; a permanent opening failure surfaces its
typed refusal. Successful handles and all other asset outcomes retain their
existing lifetime and retry rules. Kept upload observations likewise refresh
when local storage becomes executable; no user action is automatically replayed.

Callers needing `app.ready` as the old local-opening barrier explicitly select
`startup: "awaited"`. Both modes inspect and recover existing journal custody;
only the engine-opening barrier differs. An awaited compatible opening with an
empty journal and no unsettled capture may select the outbox even on a first
visit. Starters omit the option; the cards document the opt-out.

    wrappers.set(handler, wrapped);
    add(type, wrapped, options);
  });
  t.mock.method(target, "removeEventListener", (type, handler, options) => {
    assert.equal(type, "storage");
    removed.push(handler);
    remove(type, wrappers.get(handler), options);
  });
  Object.defineProperty(globalThis, "window", { configurable: true, value: target });
  const key = "snapback4.test.shared-journal.writes";
  const storageChanged = () => {
    const event = new Event("storage");
    Object.defineProperty(event, "key", { value: key });
    target.dispatchEvent(event);
  };
  let a, b;
  try {
    a = journalChanges(key, () => aNotices++);
    b = journalChanges(key, () => bNotices++);
    assert.equal(registered.length, 1, "two owners share one storage listener");
    storageChanged();
    assert.deepEqual([deliveries, aNotices, bNotices], [1, 1, 1]);
    a.close();
    assert.equal(removed.length, 0, "the first close keeps the shared listener");
    storageChanged();
    assert.deepEqual([deliveries, aNotices, bNotices], [2, 1, 2]);
    b.close();
    storageChanged();
    assert.deepEqual([deliveries, aNotices, bNotices], [2, 1, 2], "after final close the event reaches no handler or owner");
    assert.equal(removed.length, 1, "the last close removes the shared listener");
    assert.equal(removed[0], registered[0], "removal uses the registered handler");
  } finally {
    a?.close(); b?.close();
    if (previousWindow) Object.defineProperty(globalThis, "window", previousWindow);
    else delete globalThis.window;
  }
});

// Wave-3 lanes 053 063 089: the non-null viewer follows the gate's own snapshot.
test("useSignedInViewer returns the signed-in viewer and refuses E_AUTH outside a signed-in gate", async () => {
  const { createElement } = await import("react");
  const { renderToString } = await import("react-dom/server");
  const { AppProvider, SnapbackProvider, useAuth, useSignedInViewer } = await import("../dist/react.js");
  const client = viewer => ({ viewer: () => viewer, onViewer: () => () => {} });
  const app = (snapshot, clientViewer = snapshot.viewer) => ({ client: client(clientViewer), online: {}, onOnlineChange: () => () => {},
    auth: { ...snapshot, onChange: () => () => {}, getSnapshot: () => snapshot } });
  function Mine() { return createElement("p", null, useSignedInViewer()); }
  function Gate() { const auth = useAuth(); return auth.state === "signed-in" ? createElement(Mine) : createElement("p", null, auth.state); }
  const underApp = (snapshot, child, clientViewer) => renderToString(createElement(AppProvider, { app: app(snapshot, clientViewer) }, createElement(child)));
  assert.equal(underApp({ state: "signed-in", viewer: "dev:alice" }, Mine), "<p>dev:alice</p>");
  // The app's auth snapshot decides, even while the client's viewer lags it.
  assert.equal(underApp({ state: "signed-in", viewer: "dev:alice" }, Mine, null), "<p>dev:alice</p>");
  for (const state of ["restoring", "signed-out"]) {
    assert.equal(underApp({ state, viewer: null }, Gate), `<p>${state}</p>`, "a gate never renders the signed-in child");
    assert.throws(() => underApp({ state, viewer: null }, Mine, "dev:stale"), error => {
      assert.equal(error.why.code, "E_AUTH");
      assert.match(error.message, new RegExp(`auth.state is "${state}"`));
      assert.match(error.why.rewrite, /auth\.state === "signed-in"/);
      if (state === "restoring") {
        assert.match(error.message, /if \(auth\.state === "restoring"\) return <Loading \/>/);
        assert.match(error.message, /only when `auth\.state === "signed-in"`/);
      }
      return true;
    });
  }
  const underClient = viewer => renderToString(createElement(SnapbackProvider, { client: client(viewer) }, createElement(Mine)));
  assert.equal(underClient("dev:bob"), "<p>dev:bob</p>");
  assert.throws(() => underClient(null), error => error.why.code === "E_AUTH");
  assert.throws(() => renderToString(createElement(Mine)), /no <AppProvider> or <SnapbackProvider>/);
});

// @ref LLP 3000.002.000#4 — a progressive opening refusal is loading until readiness or a terminal opening failure.
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { createRequire } from 'node:module';
import { mkdtempSync, writeFileSync, rmSync } from 'node:fs';
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os';
import { join, resolve } from 'node:path';
import { createBrowserServer, loadBrowserPage } from './helpers/browser-server.mjs';
import { avatarFixture } from './helpers/avatar-fixture.mjs';
import { chromiumExecutable } from '../../../witness/lib.mjs';
import { hangBudget } from './helpers/wait.mjs';

const root = resolve(import.meta.dirname, '../../..');
test('WASM assets wait for default progressive opening, recover once, and expose permanent opening failure', { timeout: hangBudget(90) }, async t => {
  const f = await avatarFixture(t), dir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'sb4-asset-opening-'));
  const require = createRequire(join(root, 'package.json'));
  const react = createRequire(join(root, 'packages/snapback4/package.json'));
  let server, browser;
  t.after(async () => { await browser?.close(); await server?.close(); rmSync(dir, { recursive: true, force: true }); });
  writeFileSync(join(dir, 'index.html'), '<div id="root"></div><script type="module" src="/harness.jsx"></script>');
  writeFileSync(join(dir, 'harness.jsx'), harness);
  server = await createBrowserServer({ root: dir, configFile: false, logLevel: 'error', server: { host: '127.0.0.1', port: 0, fs: { allow: [root, dir] } }, resolve: { alias: [
    { find: /^react$/, replacement: react.resolve('react') },
    { find: /^react-dom\/client$/, replacement: react.resolve('react-dom/client') },
    ...['app', 'auth', 'react', 'web'].map(name => ({ find: `snapback4/${name}`, replacement: join(root, `packages/snapback4/dist/${name}.js`) })),
    { find: '#fetch', replacement: join(root, 'packages/snapback4/dist/default-fetch.js') },
  ] } });
  await server.listen();
  browser = await require('playwright-core').chromium.launch({ timeout: hangBudget(), executablePath: chromiumExecutable(), headless: true, args: ['--no-sandbox'] });
  for (const mode of ['default', 'awaited', 'failed', 'unmount', 'signout']) await t.test(mode, async t => {
    const page = await browser.newPage(); t.after(() => page.close());
    page.setDefaultTimeout(hangBudget());
    await loadBrowserPage(t, page, server.resolvedUrls.local[0]);
    await page.waitForFunction(() => window.boot);
    const options = { mode, url: f.url, session: f.users.bob.session, id: f.users.alice.avatar.id };
    if (mode === 'awaited') {
      await page.evaluate(options => { window.booted = boot(options); }, options);
      await page.waitForFunction(() => window.openEntered);
      assert.equal(await page.evaluate(() => !!window.mounted), false, 'awaited retains its opening barrier');
      await page.evaluate(() => releaseOpening()); await page.evaluate(() => booted);
    } else {
      await page.evaluate(options => boot(options), options);
      await page.waitForFunction(() => window.outcomes.some(x => x.denied?.code === 'E_STORE'));
      assert.equal(await page.evaluate(() => window.state.status), 'loading');
      assert.equal(await page.evaluate(() => window.commits.some(x => x.status === 'denied' || x.status === 'error')), false);
      if (mode === 'unmount') await page.evaluate(() => root.unmount());
      if (mode === 'signout') await page.evaluate(() => { window.signingOut = app.auth.logout(); });
      await page.evaluate(() => releaseOpening());
      if (mode === 'signout') await page.evaluate(() => signingOut);
    }
    if (mode === 'failed') {
      await page.waitForFunction(() => window.state.status === 'denied');
      assert.equal(await page.evaluate(() => window.state.why.message), 'permanent opening failure');
    } else if (mode === 'unmount' || mode === 'signout') {
      await page.evaluate(() => app.close());
      assert.equal(await page.evaluate(() => window.outcomes.filter(x => x.url).length), 0, 'retired selection never downloads after opening');
      if (mode === 'signout') assert.equal(await page.evaluate(() => window.state.why.code), 'E_AUTH');
    } else {
      await page.waitForFunction(() => window.state.status === 'ready');
      await page.waitForFunction(() => window.localSnapshot().executable && window.localSnapshot().acquired);
      assert.equal(await page.evaluate(() => window.outcomes.filter(x => x.url).length), 1, 'acquisition notifications cannot fetch another view');
    }
    await page.evaluate(() => app.close());
  });
});

};
`;

  async "useAsset never commits a previous id, client or principal's handle"() {
    const client = controlled(), replacement = controlled(), waiting = new Map(), commits = [];
    const links = new Set(); let signedOut = false;
    replacement.link = () => signedOut ? "signed-out" : "online";
    replacement.onLink = listener => { links.add(listener); return () => links.delete(listener); };
    let revoked = 0, calls = 0;
    client.asset = id => { calls++; const result = deferred(); waiting.set(id, result); return result.promise; };
    replacement.asset = client.asset;

      useLayoutEffect(() => { commits.push({ id, ...asset }); });
      return null;
    }
    const handle = id => ({ url: "blob:" + id, type: "image/png", bytes: 1, revoke: () => { revoked++; } });
    await mount(h(Probe, { id: null }), client);

    check(commits.at(-1).status === "ready", "initial asset ready");
    commits.length = 0;

    check(revoked === 1, "replacement releases old handle");
    const oldRequest = waiting.get("new");

    await render(h(Probe, { id: "new" }), replacement);
    await act(async () => waiting.get("new").resolve(handle("new")));
    check(commits.at(-1).url === "blob:new", "current client ready");
    await act(async () => oldRequest.resolve(handle("late-old-client")));
    check(commits.at(-1).status === "ready" && commits.at(-1).url === "blob:new", "obsolete completion after current readiness cannot replace it");
    check(revoked === 2, "late obsolete response released");
    await render(h(Probe, { id: null }), replacement);
    check(revoked === 3, "clearing releases the current handle");
    commits.length = 0;
    await render(h(Probe, { id: "new" }), replacement);
    check(commits.every(s => s.status === "loading"), "reselecting an id cannot revive its revoked handle");
    await act(async () => waiting.get("new").resolve(handle("new-again")));

    check(commits.length > 0 && commits.every(s => s.status === "denied" && s.why.code === "E_AUTH"), "in-place sign-out immediately hides the handle");
    check(calls === before && revoked === 4, "signed-out hook performs no fetch and releases its URL");

  async "useAsset recovers transport errors on focus and reconnect, never denials or consumed views"() {
    const client = controlled(), listeners = new Set(); let link = "online", outcome, state, calls = 0, revokes = 0;
    client.link = () => link;
    client.onLink = cb => { listeners.add(cb); return () => listeners.delete(cb); };
    client.asset = async () => { calls++; return outcome; };
    function Probe({ id }) { state = useAsset(id); return null; }
    const error = (code, retryable) => ({ denied: { code, family: "link", message: "explained", retryable } });
    const ready = () => ({ url: "blob:owned", type: "image/png", revoke() { revokes++; } });
    for (const trigger of ["focus", "reconnect"]) {

      await act(async () => {

      });

      await act(async () => window.dispatchEvent(new Event("focus")));
      equal(calls, before + 1, "ready handle is never refetched");

    await act(async () => third.set({ denied: { code: "E_RULE", family: "rule", message: "revoked" } }));
    check(latest.read.denied?.code === "E_RULE", "a later refusal is not hidden by the prefix");
    await act(async () => first.set({ loading: true }));
    check(latest.read.loading && latest.items.length === 0 && active(client).length === 1, "a first-page reset immediately discards every old page");
    await act(async () => third.set(ready(["late"], null)));
    check(latest.read.loading && latest.items.length === 0, "an old suffix cannot reappear after reset");
    await act(async () => first.set(ready([], "empty")));
    equal(latest.read.data, [], "an empty ready prefix also stays ready while the next page loads");
    await unmount(); allClosed(client);
  },
};

for (const [name, Component] of [["web", WebApp], ["Expo", ExpoApp]]) {
  cases[name + " app closes asynchronous opens before/after cleanup and ignores obsolete failures"] = async () => {
    let opens = [];
    globalThis.openClient = () => { const result = deferred(); opens.push(result); return result.promise; };
    await mount(h(Component));
    check(opens.length === 2, "Strict Mode replays the client-open effect");
    const live = controlled();
    await act(async () => { opens[0].reject(Error("obsolete open")); opens[1].resolve(live); });
    check(!host.textContent.includes("obsolete open") && !host.textContent.includes("Opening"), "only current open result renders");
    await unmount(); check(live.closes === 1, "resolved client closes on cleanup");
    opens = [];
    await mount(h(Component)); await unmount();
    const abandoned = opens.map(() => controlled());
    await act(async () => opens.forEach((open, n) => open.resolve(abandoned[n])));
    check(abandoned.every(client => client.closes === 1), "clients resolving after cleanup close immediately");
    opens = [];
    await mount(h(Component));
    await act(async () => { opens[0].reject(Error("obsolete")); opens[1].reject(Error("current open failed")); });
    check(host.textContent.includes("current open failed") && !host.textContent.includes("obsolete"), "current rejection is visible");
    await unmount();
  };
}

cases["web sign-out reports completion only after durable clearing and offers retry on failure"] = async () => {

for (const hook of ["useQuery", "usePage"]) for (const guarded of [false, true]) {
  cases[hook + " lingering remount has data in its first committed render" + (guarded ? " through the app facade" : "")] = async () => {
    let latest, queries = 0, commits = [];
    const originalNow = performance.now;
    let monotonic = originalNow.call(performance);
    const raw = createClient({ url: "http://first-commit.test", persona: "alice", fetch: async (input, init) => {
      const path = new URL(input).pathname;
      if (path === "/changes") return new Promise((_, reject) => init.signal.addEventListener("abort", () => reject(Error("closed")), { once: true }));
      if (path === "/q/read") { queries++; return Response.json({ data: ["secret"], complete: true, seq: 0 }); }
      throw Error(path);
    } });
    const facade = guarded ? guardClient(raw, async () => true, () => true, () => ({ code: "ENDED", family: "auth", message: "ended" })) : null;
    const client = facade?.client ?? raw;
    function Probe() {
      const value = hook === "useQuery" ? useQuery(query, {}, { keep: true }) : usePage(query, {}, { keep: true }).read;
      latest = value;
      useLayoutEffect(() => { commits.push({ read: value, html: host.innerHTML }); });
      return value.loading ? h("span", null, "Loading") : h("input", { defaultValue: value.data?.[0] });
    }
    try {
      await mount(h(Probe), client);
      await awaitState(async () => !(!latest.data), 'helpers/react-harness.mjs: !latest.data', { poll: async () => { await act(async () => { await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 5)); }); } });
      equal(latest.data, ["secret"], "initial query settled");
      performance.now = () => monotonic;
      await unmount();
      const before = queries, snapshot = latest;
      commits = [];
      await mount(h(Probe), client);
      equal(commits[0]?.read, snapshot, "first layout effect sees the lingering snapshot with unchanged metadata");
      check(commits[0].html.includes('value="secret"') && !commits[0].html.includes("Loading"), "first committed DOM contains the editor");
      check(commits.every(commit => !commit.read.loading), "subscription replay never commits loading either");
      equal(queries, before, "remount joins the same live watch without another read");
      await unmount();
      monotonic += 30_000;
      commits = [];
      await mount(h(Probe), client);
      check(commits[0]?.read.loading, "first commit at the exact linger cutoff starts loading, even before its timer fires");
    } finally { performance.now = originalNow; await unmount(); facade?.fence()(); await raw.close(); }
  };
}

for (const hook of ["useQuery", "usePage"]) {
  cases[hook + " createApp remount first commits the lingering answer during a held re-read"] = async () => {
    const url = "http://lingering-reread-" + hook + ".test", memory = memorySessionStore();
    await keepSession(url, { kind: "user", token: "alice", principal: "alice", expiresAt: Date.now() + 7 * 86400000 }, memory, true);
    let latest, queries = 0, commits = [], changed = false, holding = false;
    const change = deferred(), replacement = deferred();
    const app = createApp({ url, readOnly: true, sessionStore: memory, fetch: async (input, init) => {
      const path = new URL(input).pathname;
      if (path === "/schema") return Response.json({ schema: { tables: {} }, programs: [] });
      if (path === "/probe") return Response.json({ ok: true, scope: "read", viewer: "alice", store_id: "lingering-reread", seq: 0 });
      if (path === "/changes") {
        if (!changed) { changed = true; return change.promise; }
        return new Promise((_, reject) => init.signal.addEventListener("abort", () => reject(Error("closed")), { once: true }));
      }
      if (path === "/q/read") {
        queries++;
        if (holding) await replacement.promise;
        return Response.json({ data: [holding ? "replacement" : "secret"], complete: true, tables: ["notes"], seq: holding ? 1 : 0 });
      }
      throw Error(path);
    } });
    const settle = async condition => {
      // Flush React once even when the requested state is already true.
      await act(async () => { await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 5)); });
      return awaitState(condition, "lingering re-read did not settle: " + JSON.stringify({ latest, queries }), { poll: async () => { await act(async () => { await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 5)); }); } });
    };
    function Probe() {
      latest = hook === "useQuery" ? useQuery(query, {}, { keep: true }) : usePage(query, {}, { keep: true }).read;
      useLayoutEffect(() => { commits.push({ read: latest, html: host.innerHTML }); });
      return latest.loading ? h("span", null, "Loading") : h("input", { defaultValue: latest.data?.[0] });
    }
    try {
      check((await app.ready).ok, "createApp restored authority");
      await mount(h(Probe), app.client);
      await settle(() => latest.data?.[0] === "secret" && latest.fresh);
      await unmount();
      holding = true;
      change.resolve(Response.json({ tables: ["notes"], seq: 1 }));
      await settle(() => queries >= 2);
      const before = queries;
      commits = [];
      await mount(h(Probe), app.client);
      equal(commits[0]?.read.data, ["secret"], "first commit keeps the previously authorized answer");
      check(commits[0].read.fresh === true && commits[0].read.revalidating === true, "first commit preserves freshness and carries revalidation");
      check(commits[0].html.includes('value="secret"') && !commits[0].html.includes("Loading"), "the editor is in the first committed DOM");
      check(commits.every(commit => !commit.read.loading), "StrictMode subscription replay never flashes loading");
      equal(queries, before, "joining the running watch adds no duplicate read");
      replacement.resolve();
      await settle(() => latest.data?.[0] === "replacement");
    } finally {
      change.resolve(Response.json({ tables: [], seq: 1 })); replacement.resolve();
      await unmount(); await app.close();
    }
  };
}

cases["Expo observes every saved ID across reload, late refusal, unknown receipt and account switch"] = async () => {

  check(!JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key)).intents.some(i => i.id === b), "sent ID leaves the journal");

  equal(host.querySelector("input").value, "A text", "edit restores refused text as a new draft");
  await submit(); check(client.writes[3].options.id !== a, "deliberate edited send is a new intent");
  const next = controlled(); next.setViewer("dev:other");

  check(next.writes.length === 0, "no other-account resubmission"); await unmount();
};

cases["web composer fences old account callbacks and preserves saved write identities"] = async () => {
  localStorage.clear();

  b.setViewer("dev:other");
  const av = new ViewState(a, "http://starter-test", a.viewer());
  const bv = new ViewState(b, "http://starter-test", b.viewer());
  const admit = a.mutate;
  a.mutate = (op, args, options) => {
    check(av.read().intents.some(intent => intent.id === options.id), "reference is durable before SDK dispatch");
    return admit(op, args, options);
  };
  await mount(h(Composer, { key: av.key, conversationId: "a-room", view: av }), a);
  await edit("A private draft"); await submit();
  const original = av.read().intents[0].id;
  check(original.length === 26 && a.writes.length === 1 && a.writes[0].options.id === original, "saved ID is the SDK admission ID");
  av.active = false;
  await render(h(Composer, { key: bv.key, conversationId: "b-room", view: bv }), b);
  await act(async () => a.writes[0].resolve(failed(original)));
  check(!host.textContent.includes(original) && !host.textContent.includes("A private draft") && !host.textContent.includes("message refused"), "A result cannot enter B UI");
  check(b.writes.length === 0 && bv.read().intents.length === 0, "account switch does not replay A as B");
  check(av.read().intents[0].id === original, "switch preserves A reference");
  let refused = false;
  try { av.remember({ id: "late", room: "a-room", operation: "send" }); } catch { refused = true; }
  check(refused, "a delayed A callback cannot admit another reference");
  const otherBackend = new ViewState(a, "http://different-backend", a.viewer());
  check(otherBackend.read().intents.length === 0, "references do not cross backends");
  await unmount();
};
cases["receipt notifications read one pending list for ten thousand message hooks"] = async () => {
  const client = controlled(), listeners = new Set();
  let reads = 0, renders = 0, entries = [];
  client.onPendingWrites = fn => { listeners.add(fn); return () => listeners.delete(fn); };
  client.pendingWrites = async () => { reads++; return entries.map(entry => ({ ...entry })); };
  function Bubble() { const writes = usePendingWrites(mutation); renders++; return h("span", null, writes.length); }
  await mount(h("div", null, Array.from({ length: 10000 }, (_, key) => h(Bubble, { key }))), client);
  equal(listeners.size, 1, "the message history shares one pending-list subscription");
  const startReads = reads, startRenders = renders;
  for (let peer = 1; peer < 50; peer++) {
    await act(async () => { for (const notify of listeners) notify(); });
  }
  equal(reads - startReads, 49, "per-receipt work is independent of message count");
  equal(renders, startRenders, "unchanged empty outboxes do not rerender the history");
  entries = [{ id: "own", op: "write", args: {}, state: "queued", predicted: [] }];
  await act(async () => { for (const notify of listeners) notify(); });
  check([...host.querySelectorAll("span")].every(span => span.textContent === "1"), "every hook sees an admitted own write");
  entries = [];
  await act(async () => { for (const notify of listeners) notify(); });
  check([...host.querySelectorAll("span")].every(span => span.textContent === "0"), "settlement reaches every hook");
  await unmount();
  equal(listeners.size, 0, "last unmount releases the shared subscription");
};

cases["pending-write lists filter, update, fence old reads, and release StrictMode subscriptions"] = async () => {
  const listeners = new Set(), reads = [];
  let values = [], current;
  const client = controlled();
  client.onPendingWrites = fn => { listeners.add(fn); return () => listeners.delete(fn); };
  client.pendingWrites = () => { const read = deferred(); reads.push(read); return read.promise; };
  function List({ op }) { current = usePendingWrites(op); return h("div", null, current.map(w => w.id + ":" + w.state).join(",")); }
  await mount(h(List, { op: mutation }), client);
  equal(listeners.size, 1, "StrictMode leaves one listener");
  const queued = { id: "one", op: "write", args: { text: "typed" }, state: "queued", predicted: [] };
  await act(async () => { for (const read of reads.splice(0)) read.resolve([queued]); });
  equal(current, [queued], "initial queue is visible without a predicted row");
  await act(async () => { for (const notify of listeners) notify(); });
  const older = reads.pop();
  await act(async () => { for (const notify of listeners) notify(); });
  const sent = { ...queued, state: "sent" };
  await act(async () => { reads.pop().resolve([sent, { ...queued, id: "other", op: "edit" }]); });
  equal(current, [sent], "filter retains only this operation");
  await act(async () => { older.resolve([queued]); });
  equal(current, [sent], "overtaken list cannot regress dispatch");
  const held = { ...sent, state: "held", reason: "E_BUSY" };
  await act(async () => { for (const notify of listeners) notify(); });
  await act(async () => { reads.pop().resolve([held]); });
  equal(current, [held], "retryable hold is visible");
  await render(h(List), client);
  await act(async () => { reads.pop().resolve([held, { ...queued, id: "other", op: "edit" }]); });
  equal(current.length, 2, "omitting the filter lists every mutation");
  await act(async () => { for (const notify of listeners) notify(); });
  await act(async () => { reads.pop().resolve([]); });
  equal(current, [], "settlement removes writes");
  await act(async () => { for (const notify of listeners) notify(); });
  const detached = reads.pop();
  await unmount();
  equal(listeners.size, 0, "unmount releases listeners");
  await act(async () => detached.resolve([held]));
  await mount(h(List), client);
  equal(current, [], "remount cannot publish the old lifetime");
  await act(async () => { for (const read of reads.splice(0)) read.resolve([]); });
  await unmount();
};
